request: We need to hand out a yearly training budget across departments, with rules for who gets priority when it runs out.

problem: Department heads fight over the budget by email today and the loudest one wins, and finance only discovers the overspend in March.
The real cost is not the money, it is that mandatory certifications get bumped by discretionary courses and we then fail the audit.
current_process: One shared spreadsheet per department, consolidated by HR twice a year, and the two consolidations never match.
There is no reservation step at all: a manager books with the vendor first and tells HR afterwards.
success_metrics: Zero certification lapses, and finance seeing committed spend within a week of the booking rather than at year end.
We would also count it a success if HR stopped spending two weeks each January reconciling the spreadsheets.
actors: Department heads request, HR validates eligibility, finance owns the envelope, and the employee books the course.
For the three regulated entities a compliance officer has to countersign anything that is a certification renewal.
business_objects: A request carries the employee, the course, the vendor quote, the department and the fiscal year.
The envelope is an object too: an amount, a period and a scope, and it can be split by cost centre.
business_rules: Certifications outrank everything, then seniority within the department, then first come first served.
Unused budget carries over one year for the regulated entities and is lost everywhere else.
A mid-year joiner gets a pro-rata entitlement, and a leaver's committed but unspent amount returns to the envelope.
workflow: Request, eligibility check, budget reservation, approval, booking, then invoice reconciliation.
A reservation has to be able to expire: if nobody has booked within thirty days the money goes back to the pool.
permissions: A department head sees only their own envelope; HR and finance see all of them.
The compliance officer sees certification requests across every entity but must not see amounts.
integrations: Bookings come back from the vendor portal as a CSV, and the invoices land in the accounting system.
We have not decided whether the tool pushes to accounting or accounting pulls from it.
constraints: The fiscal year is not the calendar year for two of the entities, and the tool has to close within five working days of year end.
Everything has to work for a department head on a phone, because half of them are never at a desk.
config_vs_custom: Every client we roll this out to orders the priorities differently, so that has to be configurable rather than coded.
edge_cases: A vendor can cancel a course after the money is committed, and the refund can land in the next fiscal year.
Two department heads can request the last remaining seat within the same minute.
reporting: Finance needs committed versus spent versus remaining per envelope, and an audit trail of who overrode a priority.
The auditor asks for the state of an envelope as it stood on a given date, not just as it stands now.
acceptance: It is accepted when a full year can be replayed from the audit trail and matches the accounting system to the cent.
risks: The main risk is that department heads keep booking with the vendor first, and the tool then records fiction.
The second is that we roll it out mid-year and nobody can say what the opening balances should be.
